title: Lesson 54: Performance: Latency Budgets, Streaming, Batching, and Speculative Execution
description: Latency as a budget you allocate across an agent's pipeline: the two numbers that dominate, who is waiting and which number binds, and the levers (streaming, batching, speculative execution) that keep each step inside its slice.

questions.question: Which latency number matters most for a human who reads an answer as it arrives?
options: End-to-end latency, because it measures the whole response
Time to first token, because the reader stops waiting
Time per output token, because faster tokens read better
Batch size, because it sets how responsive the reply feels
questions.explanation: Once the stream outpaces reading speed, the only wait a person consciously feels is the silence before the first token. For a human reader, time to first token is the experience.

questions.question: When the consumer of a model call is another system that blocks on the full completion, what is the right move?
options: Stream the response so the machine sees tokens sooner
Lower the per-token rate as far as possible
Turn streaming off and optimize the full completion
Add batching to the single request to speed it up
questions.explanation: A downstream service cannot act on partial output, so streaming just moves the same wait around without hiding it. For a machine consumer, the binding number is end-to-end latency.

questions.question: Why does continuous batching outperform static batching?
options: It admits and evicts work at each decode step to keep the GPU busy
It runs each request on a separate GPU with no sharing
It removes the need for any latency budget at all
It keeps every request in a single batch until all of them have finished
questions.explanation: Static batching holds a whole set together until its slowest member finishes, wasting time as output lengths vary. Continuous batching fills freed slots at every decode step, keeping the GPU busy and freeing short requests early.
